reasoning_traces.think: Chapter 3 explores pitch sequencing through directed graph embeddings, focusing on setup and knockout pitches. The core idea is that pitch sequences can be modeled as directed graphs where nodes are pitch types and edges represent transition probabilities. Setup pitches are those that precede a strategic outcome, while knockout pitches are those that terminate a sequence with a favorable result. The identification process uses frequency thresholds to ensure statistical relevance, preventing rare pitches from skewing the analysis. The paper emphasizes that knockout pitches are not necessarily the most effective pitches but rather those that end sequences effectively. The mathematical foundation lies in computing forward dependency differentials between pitch pairs, which quantify the influence of one pitch on another. This approach enables the detection of strategic patterns in pitch selection and sequencing. The framework distinguishes between local sinks (single pitch knockout) and global sinks (multiple pitch knockout), allowing for nuanced tactical analysis. The paper also notes that not all clusters contain knockout pitches, indicating some sequences lack clear terminal points. This observation leads to a deeper understanding of pitch sequencing complexity and variability across different pitcher profiles. The implications extend beyond simple categorization to include real-time decision support systems for coaches and analysts.

The framework also supports visualization of sequencing behavior through graph networks, providing intuitive tools for scouts and analysts.
